messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anh Nguyen was sixty years old, a fisherman who had worked the Pacific waters since he was a boy in Vietnam and later off the coast of Oregon, where he and his younger brother, Bao, had built a modest life as deckhands on a charter boat. The accident happened on a late autumn morning two years ago. A squall came up fast while they were running lines about twelve miles out, and the boat took a wave over the stern. Bao was coiling a rope near the rail when the deck tilted. Anh saw him slip, saw his hands grab for nothing, and then the water swallowed him. Anh dove in after him, but the current was brutal and the visibility near zero. He surfaced once, twice, and then couldn't find Bao again. The Coast Guard recovered Bao's body three days later. The official report said hypothermia and drowning; the weather had been unpredictable but forecasted as manageable. Anh never said it aloud, but he knew the truth: he should have held on tighter, should have made Bao wear a life jacket, should have turned back sooner. That certainty lived in him like a second skeleton.

In the months that followed, Anh did not stop working, but the work itself became a kind of assault. The moment he stepped onto the dock, his chest would tighten and his hands would shake. Certain sounds—the creak of a line, the slap of water against a hull—sent a jolt through him that he could not control. He would feel a rush of heat and then a cold dread, and he would have to sit down or grip something solid to keep from falling. He learned to scan every wave as if it might rise up and take someone else. He stopped going out on rough days, then on any day with a wind over ten knots, and eventually he refused to work past the jetty. His captain grew frustrated, and Anh did not blame him. He had come to believe that no one could be trusted with safety—not the weather service, not the boat owners, not the other men who joked about the sea like it was a pet. He kept his distance from the crew at the fish house, turning away when they asked about Bao, because he was certain that if they knew the full story they would see what he saw: a man who had let his brother die.

At home, he moved through the days mechanically. His wife, Linh, would speak to him and he would hear the words but feel nothing behind them. He had stopped feeling much of anything except a low, constant shame. Sometimes a wave of anger would rise up—at the ocean, at the boat, at himself—and then it would fall away into a hollow numbness that frightened him more. He could not cry. He could not laugh. He lay awake night after night staring at the ceiling, replaying the moment of Bao's hand slipping away, and when sleep finally came it was thin and broken. Linh found him sitting on the edge of the bed at three in the morning, his breath fast, his skin cold. He told her it was nothing, but he was thinking that he should not have come back at all. The guilt sat in his chest like a stone: Bao had a wife and a young daughter, and Anh had nothing to offer them but a dead brother's memory. What kind of man survives when his little brother does not?

He stopped going to family gatherings. He stopped answering the phone when Bao's widow called. He stopped walking past the memorial photo Linh had placed on the shelf. Each avoidance made the world smaller, but it also made the world feel safer—or at least less likely to spring another reminder on him. The consequence was that Linh began to cry in the kitchen, quietly, and then one evening she told him that she could not watch him disappear any longer. She had made an appointment at the community mental health clinic. He went because he was afraid of losing her too, but also because a part of him—a very small, buried part—was tired of feeling dead. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, trying not to listen to the sound of the rain against the window, because it sounded exactly like the waves that night.
